newsitem.title: EU: EP COMMITTEE DEBATES NATO ENLARGEMENT WITH JAVIER SOLANA.
newsitem.headline: EP COMMITTEE DEBATES NATO ENLARGEMENT WITH JAVIER SOLANA.

text.p: EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT NEWS REPORT PRESS RELEASE
NATO ENLARGEMENT - BETWEEN THREE AND FIVE NEW MEMBERS

Replying to a question from a member of the Foreign Affairs Committee (chairman: Tom SPENCER, EPP, UK), the NATO Secretary-General, Mr Javier SOLANA, expressed the hope that the 16 NATO member states would reach agreement on enlargement either before or at the NATO enlargement summit to be held in Madrid in July 1997. He thought NATO would accept between three and five new members: Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic plus, possibly, Slovenia and Romania. "At the moment, no-one is talking about more than five or less than three". Mr SOLANA said that no decision had yet been taken, since "several European countries and the USA are in favour of three new members, while others are calling for four or five". A number of MEPs expressed surprise at this reduction in the number initially expected to join, while Daniel COHN-BENDIT (Greens, D) claimed that a deal had been done with Russia under which the first wave of accessions would include only Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic. In reply, Mr SOLANA pointed out that rapid enlargement to bring in a large number of countries would lead to financial and organizational problems. In that case, asked Mr SPENCER and several other MEPs, why not set a timetable for a second wave of accessions? "I don't think we will be quite so precise after the first wave ... we can't lay down a fixed timetable ... above all, we will have to assess the first enlargement", answered Mr SOLANA. Mr SPENCER hoped that the second stage would begin as swiftly as possible: at the latest, immediately after the ratification procedures on the first wave.

Mr SOLANA was more optimistic than the MEPs regarding Russia's reactions. First of all, he pointed out, the Russians had no veto over NATO's enlargement and in any case they had no objections to Romania and Slovenia becoming members. He welcomed the partnership agreement with Russia and thought that the Duma would not hold up the START II agreements as a way of expressing its fears about NATO enlargement. "I have the feeling that ratification of START II will go hand-in-hand with the START III negotiations. We are moving towards ratification of START II."

When pressed by MEPs to state the cost of enlargement, Mr SOLANA refused to engage in this kind of exercise. "The figures circulating in the press go far beyond our calculations", he said. To speak about this now would amount to taking a decision on certain countries already. Having said that, there would clearly be costs but these were "bearable". They would include the cost of pooling resources (he felt that NATO's experience in Bosnia in this regard had been useful) and costs to be borne by the applicant countries themselves (although these would be lower than if the countries in question did not join).

The NATO Secretary General also stressed the importance of the European defence pillar within the Atlantic Alliance and recalled, in this connection, the decisions taken at Berlin in 1996 by the NATO foreign ministers. This arrangement gave the Europeans the chance to act on their own responsibility via the WEU.
Lastly, he hoped that the conclusions of the Amsterdam Summit in this area would be positive and stressed that the two enlargements were complementary, although not actually linked.
